practiceActivities.rule:
You meet someone at school.

Be tells us who or where someone is.

It also tells us how someone feels.

Use am with I.

Use is with he, she and it.

Use are with you, we and they.

I am a student.

Emma is a teacher. She is a teacher.

Ben is here. He is here.

We are at school.

It is sunny.

Use it for the weather.

For questions, put am, is or are first.

You are ready.

Are you ready?

Yes, I am.

No, I am not.

Answer with I when someone asks about you.

To say no, add not after be.

I am not ready.

Where is Emma?

She is at school.

Short forms:

I'm = I am.

Isn't = is not.

Aren't = are not.

Keep am in Yes, I am.

Wrong: Do you are ready?

Write Are you ready? Put be first.

Study: Read these two sentences.

You are ready.

Are you ready?

Which words change places?

practiceActivities.rule:
It is Friday. Ken decided last week to play volleyball on Saturday. Mia asks about his plan.

We use be going to for a plan we made before speaking. Use am, is or are + going to + a base verb. A base verb is the simple verb, like play, watch or buy.

A pronoun takes the place of a name, like he for Ken. Use am with I. Use is with he, she and it. Use are with you, we and they. Keep going to and the base verb the same.

For a question, put am, is or are before the person. For a negative, put not after am, is or are.

Ken: I am going to play volleyball tomorrow.

Mia: Are you going to play volleyball tomorrow?

Ken: Yes, I am.

A no answer is No, I'm not. You changes to I when you answer about yourself.

The negative changes the meaning: I am not going to play volleyball tomorrow.

Change the person:

Is Ken going to play? Yes, he is. No, he isn't.

Is Mia going to play? Yes, she is. No, she isn't.

Are Ken and Mia going to play? Yes, they are. No, they aren't.

No, he's not and No, she's not are also correct. So is No, they're not. Use the long form after yes: Yes, I am, not Yes, I'm.

For more information, put a question word before am, is or are.

What are you going to do tomorrow?

I'm going to play volleyball.

What asks about the activity; the answer gives the plan.

Do not leave out be: I going to play is wrong. Do not use do or does in these questions. Keep the base verb: She is going to play, not She is going to plays.

practiceActivities.rule:
At the game, Ken says: Oh no, I forgot my water!

Mia says: I'll give you some of mine. She decides now.

Use will for a decision made now, an offer or a promise. An offer is when we say we can help someone. A promise is when we say we will really do something.

The form is will + a base verb. Will stays the same for every person. I will help becomes She will help.

For a question, put will before the person. For a negative, use will not or won't.

Statement: You will bring water.

Question: Will you bring water?

Short answers: Yes, I will. No, I won't. No, I will not.

Negative: I will not bring water. I won't bring water.

Again, you changes to I when you answer about yourself.

Change the person:

Will Ken help? Yes, he will. No, he won't.

Will Mia help? Yes, she will. No, she won't.

Will Ken and Mia help? Yes, they will. No, they won't.

For more information, put a question word before will.

When will you bring the water?

I'll bring it after the game.

When asks about time.

Your bag looks heavy. I'll carry it for you. This is an offer.

I'll call you after the game. This is a promise.

Do not add -s or to after will. She will helps and She will to help are wrong. Do you will help? is also wrong. Use Will you help?

Compare these answers when Mia says: We need more balls for practice.

Ken: I know. I'm going to bring two from home.

Ken: Oh, OK. I'll bring two from home.

The first answer shows an earlier plan. The second shows a decision now. The forms often overlap when we talk about the future.

A prediction is what we think will happen. Our team will win and Our team is going to win can both be correct. With a sign now, we often choose going to. Look at those dark clouds. It's going to rain.

practiceActivities.title: Practice: Spelling the Short Forms I'll, We'll and Won't

items.prompt: Tomorrow ___ meet at the park.
items.explanation: We will becomes we'll, with an apostrophe in place of wi.

items.prompt: I ___ forget your birthday. I promise.
items.explanation: Will not becomes won't, with an apostrophe between n and t.

items.instruction: Match the long form with its short form.
items.explanation: An apostrophe shows where letters are missing in these short forms.

items.instruction: Make a sentence.
items.sourceJa: 私たちはバスに遅れません。
items.answer: We won't be late for the bus
items.explanation: Write won't with an apostrophe between n and t.

items.sentence: Ill bring the snacks on Saturday.
items.explanation: I will becomes I'll, but ill means sick.

items.prompt: (we will) ___ see you at the gym.
items.hint: Write the two words as one short form.
items.explanation: We will becomes we'll.

items.prompt: Don't worry, I ___ tell your secret. (will not)
items.hint: Write the special short form with an apostrophe.
items.explanation: Will not becomes won't.

items.instruction: Use short forms for I will and the negative.
items.source: I will text you, and we will not be late.
accepted: I'll text you, and we won't be late.
I'll text you, and we'll not be late.
items.explanation: Use I'll, then won't or we'll not for the negative.

practiceActivities.rule:
In speaking and messages to friends, we often use short forms. An apostrophe shows where letters are missing. It is a small mark at the top of the letters.

I will becomes I'll, and we will becomes we'll. Each apostrophe takes the place of wi.

Will not becomes won't. This spelling is special: will changes to wo, and not becomes n't. The apostrophe takes the place of the o in not. Do not write willn't.

I'll see you on Saturday.

We'll bring the ball.

I won't be late.

They'll wait for us at the door.

Keep the apostrophe: well and ill are different words. Ill means sick.

Use the long form after yes: Yes, I will, not Yes, I'll. After no, won't is correct: No, I won't.

targets.label: must not or don't have to?
The base verb after a modal

items.prompt: The baker is a woman. Her early start is necessary. Does the baker have to start before sunrise? Give a positive short answer using he or she: ___
items.explanation: Use she for the baker and does in the short answer.

items.instruction: Make a yes/no question using have to. Keep every other word.
items.source: The players have to book the court.
accepted: Do the players have to book the court?
items.explanation: Use Do before a plural subject in a have to question.

items.prompt: A visitor asks a guard: Must I leave the emergency exit clear? Complete the guard's positive short answer: ___
items.explanation: The guard answers with you for the visitor and keeps must.

items.instruction: Use Visitors and must not or mustn't. Keep the action lean out of this window.
items.source: The safety rule forbids leaning out of this window.
accepted: Visitors must not lean out of this window.
Visitors mustn't lean out of this window.
items.explanation: Put not after must to express a rule against an action.

You do not have to ask for a printed receipt.

items.explanation: Spell the base verb wash after must.

items.explanation: The base verb drive ends in e.

items.explanation: You changes to I, and the negative short answer uses don't or do not.

items.instruction: Make this action not necessary using a negative form of have to. Keep every other word.
items.source: We have to print the tickets.
accepted: We don't have to print the tickets.
We do not have to print the tickets.
items.explanation: Use don't have to or do not have to with we.

items.instruction: A lifeguard says this to the swimmers. Make the swimmers' yes/no question using we. Keep must and shower before entering.
items.explanation: Change you to we and put must before we.

items.prompt: Everyone must turn off their phone during the recording. She ___ turn off her phone too.
items.explanation: Must stays the same with she.

items.prompt: Complete with a form of must or have to: The quiz rules forbid help from other teams. You ___ look at another team's answers.
items.explanation: Must not and mustn't both express a forbidden action.

items.prompt: At the art club, aprons are optional. Members ___ wear aprons.
items.explanation: Don't have to leaves members a choice.

items.prompt: Type the verb for 選ぶ: Each diner must ___ one main dish.
items.explanation: The base verb choose has oo and ends in e.

items.instruction: Correct the spelling of the action word. Keep every other word.
items.explanation: Spell the base verb feed with ee.

items.source: I have to send the invoice today.

items.explanation: Have to changes to has to with the accountant.

items.prompt: The library assistant is a man. Returning the key tonight is optional. Does the library assistant have to return it tonight? Give a negative short answer using he or she: ___
items.explanation: Use he for the assistant and doesn't or does not in the short answer.

items.instruction: Make a yes/no question. Keep must and every other word.

accepted: Must the photographer move the lights?
items.explanation: Put must before the subject without do or does.

items.explanation: Form the negative with must not.

items.explanation: Don't have to means guests can choose.

items.instruction: Use You and a form of must or have to. Keep the action move another player's piece.
items.source: The game rules forbid moving another player's piece.
accepted: You must not move another player's piece.
You mustn't move another player's piece.

practiceActivities.title: Practice: Have To and Has To

items.prompt: She ___ carry the class bag.
items.explanation: Use has to with she.

items.prompt: ___ he have to buy a ticket?
items.explanation: Use Does with he in a have to question.

items.instruction: Match each question with its short answer.
pairs: Do you have to bring lunch?
Does Mia have to carry the bag?
Does he have to buy a ticket?
Do we have to bring a camera?
items.explanation: Use do or does in a short answer to a have to question.

items.instruction: Make a sentence.
items.sourceJa: 彼は切符を買う必要はありません。
items.answer: He doesn't have to buy a ticket.
items.explanation: Doesn't have to means an action is not necessary.

items.sentence: Does she has to carry the class bag?
items.explanation: Use have after does.

items.prompt: Use a negative form of have to: I ___ bring a camera.
items.hint: The subject is I, and the action is not necessary.
items.explanation: Use don't have to or do not have to with I.

items.instruction: Make a yes/no question using have to. Keep every other word.
accepted: Do we have to bring lunch?
items.explanation: Put Do before we to make a have to question.

practiceActivities.rule:
Your class is getting ready for a trip.

An action is necessary when you must do it. Use have to for necessary actions. Use have to with I, you, we and they. Use has to with he, she, it or one person's name. Add a base verb: the simple form, like bring.

Start a question with Do or Does. Then put the person before have to + base verb. Use Do with I, you, we and they. Use Does with he, she, it or one name. In a short answer, use do or does without repeating the action.

I have to bring lunch.

Do you have to bring lunch? Yes, I do. / No, I do not.

Mia has to carry the class bag.

Does she have to carry the class bag? Yes, she does. / No, she does not.

Mia does not have to bring a camera.

When someone asks you about yourself, answer with I. For Mia, use she; for a boy's name, use he. For a full negative, use do not have to or does not have to. The action is not necessary. Do not becomes don't; does not becomes doesn't.

After does or doesn't, have stays have, never has. Do not add am, is or are before have to.

practiceActivities.title: Practice: Must and Must Not

items.prompt: She ___ listen to the teacher.
items.explanation: Must stays the same with she.

items.prompt: ___ we wait here?
items.explanation: Put must before the person without do or does.

items.instruction: Match each sentence or question with its meaning or answer.
items.explanation: Must means necessary, and must not means forbidden.

items.instruction: Make a sentence.
items.sourceJa: 彼はバスのドアを開けてはいけません。
items.answer: He must not open the bus door.
items.explanation: Put not after must to say an action is forbidden.

items.sentence: He musts stay together with the class.
items.explanation: Must has the same form with he.

items.prompt: Use a negative form of must: You ___ run near the road.
items.hint: The action is forbidden.
items.explanation: Must not and mustn't mean the same thing.

items.instruction: Change She to He and make a yes/no question. Keep must and every other word.
items.source: She must listen to the teacher.
accepted: Must he listen to the teacher?
items.explanation: Put must before he without changing must.

practiceActivities.rule:
Before the class leaves, the teacher gives the rules.

Must is also for necessary actions. Use it when you tell someone what they must do. You also see it in written rules. Use person + must + base verb. Must stays the same with I, you, he, she, it, we and they.

For questions, put must before the person. For an answer with yes, use the person + must. For negatives, use must not or mustn't: do not do the action.

We must stay together.

Must we stay together? Yes, you must.

She must listen to the teacher.

She must not open the bus door.

He mustn't open the bus door.

The class asks the teacher, so we becomes you in the answer. When she changes to he, must and must not stay the same.

Do not add do or does to a must question. Use Must we wait here?, never Do we must wait here? Questions with have to are more common in everyday conversation.

practiceActivities.title: Practice: Must Not or Do Not Have To

items.prompt: Touching the museum objects is forbidden. You ___ touch them.
items.explanation: Mustn't means an action is forbidden.

items.prompt: The drawing activity is optional. She ___ join it.
items.explanation: Doesn't have to means she can choose.

items.instruction: Match each sentence with its meaning.
items.explanation: Must, mustn't and don't have to express different meanings.

items.instruction: Make a sentence.
items.sourceJa: その絵を描く活動に参加する必要はありません。
items.answer: You don't have to join the drawing activity.
items.explanation: Don't have to means the activity is optional.

items.sentence: She don't have to join the drawing activity.
items.explanation: Use doesn't have to with she for an optional action.

items.prompt: The drawing activity is optional. Use a negative form of have to: We ___ join.
items.hint: An optional action leaves you a choice.
items.explanation: Don't have to and do not have to both leave a choice.

items.instruction: Use You and must not or mustn't. Keep the action touch the old objects.
items.source: Touching the old objects is forbidden.
accepted: You must not touch the old objects.
You mustn't touch the old objects.
items.explanation: Use must not or mustn't when an action is forbidden.

practiceActivities.rule:
The class visits a museum. Its rules forbid touching the old things. To forbid something is to say it is not allowed. The museum also offers a drawing activity. Joining is optional: you can choose.

Use must not for a forbidden action. Use do not have to when an action is not necessary. Use doesn't have to with he, she or it.

You must not touch the old things.

She mustn't touch the old things.

You don't have to join the drawing activity.

She doesn't have to join the drawing activity.

Must I join the drawing activity? No, you do not have to.

The last answer gives you a choice: you can join. An answer with must not says joining is forbidden. It cannot mean that joining is optional. In everyday conversation, Do I have to join? is more common than Must I join?

Do not use don't have to for the museum's rule about touching. It says touching is not necessary. It does not say touching is forbidden.

items.prompt: He must ___ the bag.
items.explanation: Use the base verb carry after must.

items.instruction: Match each verb with its correct spelling after must.
items.explanation: Use the base verb without an s ending after must.

items.instruction: Make a sentence.
items.sourceJa: 彼女はそのドアを閉めなければなりません。
items.explanation: Must is followed by the base verb without to.
Use the base verb write after must.

items.prompt: Type the action word for 聞く: We must ___ carefully.
items.hint: Think about the letters you do not hear.
items.explanation: The base verb listen keeps its silent t.

items.prompt: Type the action word for 書く: She must ___ her name.
items.hint: Think about the letter at the end of the base verb.
items.explanation: The base verb write keeps its final e.

items.prompt: Type the action word for 運ぶ: They must ___ the class bag.
items.hint: Keep the ending of the base verb.
items.explanation: The base verb carry keeps its y.

items.instruction: Replace has to with must. Keep every other word.
items.source: She has to leave with the class.
accepted: She must leave with the class.
items.explanation: Must takes a base verb without to.

practiceActivities.rule:
The teacher checks the class before the journey home. Now look at the action words.

Must is a modal: a helping verb with its own form rules. After must, use the base verb. Do not add to or an ending for he or she.

She must carry the bag.

He must write his name.

We must leave together.

You must listen carefully.

She must close the door.

The spelling stays carry, write, leave, listen and close after must. Keep the y in carry. Keep the final e in write, leave and close. Listen has a t, although you do not hear it.

Compare She has to carry the bag and She doesn't have to carry the bag. Have changes to has in the first sentence. After doesn't, use have. In both sentences, carry stays in its base form. A common mistake is adding s to carry after must.
